title: Spinal Motor Neurons
intro: Alpha motor neurons in the spinal cord and brainstem are the final common path of the nervous system: every movement is a pattern of their spikes. Each one drives a group of muscle fibres, a motor unit, and fires roughly one muscle twitch per spike. They are large cells with huge dendritic trees and strong persistent inward currents that let them amplify and prolong their input, and their recruitment by size gives smooth control of force.

items: Morphology: somata of 30 to 70 µm in the ventral horn, about 10 dendrites branching over a millimetre or more, receiving tens of thousands of synapses; a large myelinated axon leaving through the ventral root to a muscle.

Motor units: one motor neuron and the muscle fibres it innervates, from a handful (eye muscles) to over a thousand (large leg muscles). Slow units (type S) are small, fatigue-resistant and have small motor neurons; fast fatigable units (FF) are large with large motor neurons.

Size principle: as input increases, motor neurons are recruited from smallest to largest, because small cells have higher input resistance and reach threshold first (Henneman 1957; Henneman, Somjen & Carpenter 1965). Force is graded by recruitment and by rate coding.

Firing: a nearly linear f-I relation in the primary range, steeper secondary range at higher currents; a long after-hyperpolarisation (50 to 150 ms, longer in slow units) from SK channels sets the typical rates of about 5 to 30 Hz in human voluntary contraction.

Persistent inward currents (PICs): dendritic L-type calcium (Cav1.3) and persistent sodium currents, enabled by serotonin and noradrenaline from the brainstem, amplify synaptic input up to about fivefold and can produce plateau potentials that keep the cell firing after the input ends, and hysteresis between recruitment and de-recruitment (Hounsgaard & Kiehn 1989; Heckman et al. 2005).

Inputs: direct monosynaptic input from muscle spindle Ia afferents (the stretch reflex), corticospinal input (direct in primates for hand muscles), spinal interneurons including central pattern generators for locomotion, and recurrent inhibition through Renshaw cells.

Booth, Rinzel and Kiehn (1997): a two-compartment model (soma with Na, K-dr, N-type Ca and Ca-activated K; dendrite with L-type Ca and Ca-activated K) of turtle motor neurons. It reproduces plateau potentials, bistable firing and serotonin-dependent hysteresis, and is the standard reduced motor neuron model.

Traub (1977) and Dodge and Cooley (1973): early compartmental motor neuron models. Fleshman, Segev and Burke (1988) built passive models from reconstructed cat motor neurons that set the standard for dendritic cable analysis.
Elbasiouny, Bennett and Mushahwar (2005) and Powers, Elbasiouny, Rymer and Heckman (2012): detailed models with dendritic PICs, used to explain amplification and hysteresis in human motor units.

Motor pool models: Fuglevand, Winter and Patla (1993) simulated a pool of 120 motor units with size-ordered thresholds and rate coding to reproduce force and EMG; it is still the standard model for EMG and force simulation.

Integrate-and-fire motor neurons with adaptation and a long AHP, and conductance-based pools (Cisi & Kohn 2008, the ReMoto simulator), are used in neuromechanical simulations of reflexes and locomotion.

blocks.source:
Size principle in a motor pool (after Fuglevand et al. 1993)

unit i = 1..N   recruitment threshold  RTE_i = exp( ln(RR) · i / N )
                (RR ≈ 30: largest unit needs ~30× the drive of the smallest)
rate    f_i(E) = min( f_min + g · (E - RTE_i),  f_max )   when E ≥ RTE_i
twitch  peak force P_i ∝ exp( ln(RP) · i / N )   (RP ≈ 100)
force   F(t) = Σ_i  twitch_i * spikes_i(t)      (with saturation at high rate)

blocks.text: What this means for your SNN

items: If your network drives a body or a robot, a pool of output neurons with size-ordered thresholds converts a common drive into smooth, graded force: recruitment for coarse changes, rate for fine ones.
Plateau potentials are a natural, cheap way to hold a posture without constant input: a dendritic compartment with a persistent current turns a brief command into sustained firing.
A long after-hyperpolarisation limits rates to the useful range and makes firing regular, which is what muscles need.
